'''''Adansonia digitata''''', the '''African baobab''', is the most widespread tree species of the genus ''[[Adansonia]]'', the baobabs, and is native to the African continent and the southern Arabian Peninsula (Yemen, Oman). These are long-lived [[pachycaul]]s; [[radiocarbon dating]] has shown at least one individual to be 1,275 years old. They are typically found in dry, hot [[savanna]]s of [[sub-Saharan Africa]], where they dominate the landscape and reveal the presence of a watercourse from afar. They have traditionally been valued as sources of food, water, health remedies or places of shelter and are a key food source for many animals. They are steeped in legend and superstition. In recent years, many of the largest, oldest trees have died, for unknown reasons. Other common names for the baobab include '''monkey-bread tree''', '''upside-down tree''', and '''cream of tartar tree'''.

==Description==

African baobabs are trees that often grow as solitary individuals, and are large and distinctive elements of [[savanna]] or [[scrubland]] vegetation. They grow to a height of {{Convert|5–25|m|abbr=off}}.<ref name=wick>{{cite book | last=Wickens | first=G.E. | title=The Baobabs: Pachycauls of Africa, Madagascar and Australia | publisher=Springer Science & Business Media | publication-place=Berlin] [New York | date=2008-03-02 | isbn=978-1-4020-6431-9 | pages=31–}}</ref> The trunk is typically very broad and fluted or cylindrical, often with a buttressed, spreading base.<ref name="Baum">{{cite journal | last=Baum | first=David A. | title=A Systematic Revision of Adansonia (Bombacaceae) | journal=Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden | publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden Press | volume=82 | issue=3 | year=1995 | issn=0026-6493 | jstor=2399893 | pages=440–471 | doi=10.2307/2399893 | bibcode=1995AnMBG..82..440B }}</ref> Trunks may reach a diameter of {{Convert|10–14|m|abbr=on}},<ref name="Baum"/> and may be made up of multiple stems fused around a hollow core.<ref name= Patrut>{{cite journal | last1=Patrut | first1=Adrian | last2=Woodborne | first2=Stephan | last3=von Reden | first3=Karl F. | last4=Hall | first4=Grant | last5=Hofmeyr | first5=Michele | last6=Lowy | first6=Daniel A. | last7=Patrut | first7=Roxana T. | title=African Baobabs with False Inner Cavities: The Radiocarbon Investigation of the Lebombo Eco Trail Baobab | journal=PLOS ONE | volume=10 | issue=1 | date=2015-01-26 | issn=1932-6203 | pmid=25621989 | pmc=4306539 | doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0117193 | doi-access=free | article-number=e0117193| bibcode=2015PLoSO..1017193P }}</ref> The hollow core found in many tree species is the result of wood removal, such as decay of the oldest, internal part of the trunk. In baobabs, however, many of the largest and oldest of the trees have a hollow core that is the result of a fused circle of three to eight stems sprouting from roots.<ref name= Patrut/> The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is grey and usually smooth. The main branches can be massive. All baobabs are deciduous, losing their [[leaves]] in the dry season, and remaining leafless for about eight months of the year. Flowers are large, white and hanging. The fruit are rounded with a thick shell.<ref name="Baum"/>

The leaves are [[palmately compound]] with five to seven (sometimes up to nine) [[leaflet (botany)|leaflet]]s in mature trees, but seedlings and regenerating shoots may have [[simple leaves]]. The transition to compound leaves comes with age and may be gradual. African baobabs produce simple leaves much longer than most other ''Adansonia'' species. Leaflets are stalkless (sessile) to short-stalked and size is variable.<ref name="Baum"/>

Flowering occurs in both the dry and the wet season.<ref name="Baum"/> Buds are rounded with a cone-shaped tip. Flowers are showy and sometimes paired, but usually produced singly at the end of a hanging stalk about  {{Convert|15-90|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} in length. The [[calyx (botany)|calyx]] is typically made up of five (sometimes three) green triangular bent-back lobes (sepals) with a cream-coloured, hairy interior. The petals are white, roughly the same width and length – up to {{Convert|8|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}}, and are crumpled in bud.<ref name="Baum"/> Flowers open during the late afternoon, staying open and fertile for only one night.<ref name=hank>{{cite web |last1=Hankey |first1=Andrew |title=Adansonia digitata A L. | date= February 2004 |url=http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantab/adansondigit.htm |website=PlantZAfrica.com |access-date=28 November 2015}}</ref> The fresh flowers have a sweet scent, but after about 24 hours, they start to turn brown and emit a carrion smell.<ref name=hank/> The [[androecium]] is white and made up of a {{Convert|3-6|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long tube of fused [[stamen]]s (a staminal tube) surrounded by unfused (free) [[Stamen#filament|filaments]] 3–5 cm long. There are a large number of stamens, 720–1,600 per flower, with reports of up to 2,000.<ref>{{ cite book | last=Jaeger | first= Paul | date= 1961 |  title= The Wonderful Life of Flowers | location= New York | publisher= E. P. Dutton & Co. | page= 163 }}</ref> Styles are white, growing through the staminal tube and projecting beyond it. They are usually bent at right-angles and topped with an irregular [[stigma (botany)|stigma]]. Pollen grains are spherical with spikes over the surface, typical of the Malvaceae family. Pollen grain diameter is around 50 microns.<ref name="cron">{{cite journal | last1=Cron | first1=G.V. | last2=Karimi | first2=N. | last3=Glennon | first3=K.L. | last4=Udeh | first4=C. | last5=Witkowski | first5=E.T.F. | last6=Venter | first6=S.M. | last7=Assogbadio | first7=A. | last8=Baum | first8=D.A. | title=One African baobab species or two? A re-evaluation of Adansonia kilima | journal=South African Journal of Botany | volume=103 | date=2016 | doi=10.1016/j.sajb.2016.02.036 | page=312| doi-access=free | bibcode=2016SAJB..103S.312C }}</ref>

All ''Adansonia'' develop large rounded [[indehiscent]] fruit which can be up to {{convert|25|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long with a woody outer shell. African baobab fruit are quite variable in shape, from nearly round to cylindrical. The shell is {{Convert|6-10|mm|frac=8}} thick.<ref name="Baum"/> Inside is a fleshy, light beige coloured pulp. As it dries, the pulp hardens into a crumbly powder.<ref name="kempe">{{cite journal | last1=Kempe | first1=Andreas | last2=Neinhuis | first2=Christoph | last3=Lautenschläger | first3=Thea | title=''Adansonia digitata'' and ''Adansonia gregorii'' fruit shells serve as a protection against high temperatures experienced during wildfires | journal=Botanical Studies | volume=59 | issue=1 | date=2018 | issn=1999-3110 | pmid=29455307 | pmc=5816730 | doi=10.1186/s40529-018-0223-0 | doi-access=free | page=7| bibcode=2018BotSt..59....7K }}</ref> The seeds are hard and kidney-shaped with a 0.06-mm-thick coat.<ref name="kempe"/> They show long-term dormancy, only germinating after fire or passing through an animal's digestive tract.<ref name="kempe"/> It is thought that this is because the seed coat needs to be cracked or thinned to allow to water to penetrate before the seed can germinate.<ref name="kempe"/>

=== Water storage ===
Baobab trees store water in their trunks and branches on a seasonal basis as they live in areas of sustained drought and water inaccessibility. The U-shaped branches allow for water to trickle down, allowing for maximum absorption over an extended period of time even after the rain stops.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Adaptations of the Baobab Tree |url=https://sciencing.com/adaptations-baobab-tree-8344865.html |access-date=2022-06-07 |website=Sciencing |date=13 March 2018 |language=en}}</ref> The water is absorbed into the [[vascular tissue]] of the tree, where it can be moved into the tree's [[Ground tissue|parenchyma]] cells for long-term storage, or used.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chapotin |first1=S. M. |last2=Razanameharizaka |first2=J. H. |last3=Holbrook |first3=N. M. |date=2006-09-01 |title=A biomechanical perspective on the role of large stem volume and high water content in baobab trees (Adansonia spp.; Bombacaceae) |journal=American Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=93 |issue=9 |pages=1251–1264 |doi=10.3732/ajb.93.9.1251 |pmid=21642189 |issn=0002-9122|doi-access=free |bibcode=2006AmJB...93.1251C }}</ref> A large Baobab can store as much as 136,400 liters of water.<ref>{{cite book | last1= Palmer | first1= Eve | last2= Pitman |first2= Norah | date= 1972 | title= Trees of South Africa-Volume 2 |  location= Cape Town | publisher= A.A. Balkema | page= 1459 }}</ref>

During the dry season, the trees expel all of their leaves.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Chapotin |first1=Saharah Moon |last2=Razanameharizaka |first2=Juvet H. |last3=Holbrook |first3=N. Michele |date=June 2006 |title=Water relations of baobab trees (Adansonia spp. L.) during the rainy season: does stem water buffer daily water deficits? |journal=Plant, Cell and Environment |language=en |volume=29 |issue=6 |pages=1021–1032 |bibcode=2006PCEnv..29.1021C |doi=10.1111/j.1365-3040.2005.01456.x |issn=0140-7791 |pmid=17080930 |doi-access=free}}</ref> During this period, the circumference of the trunk will shrink about 2–3 cm and the water content of the stem will drop by about 10%.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Chapotin |first1=Saharah Moon |last2=Razanameharizaka |first2=Juvet H. |last3=Holbrook |first3=N. Michele |date=February 2006 |title=Baobab trees ( Adansonia ) in Madagascar use stored water to flush new leaves but not to support stomatal opening before the rainy season |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1469-8137.2005.01618.x |journal=New Phytologist |language=en |volume=169 |issue=3 |pages=549–559 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.2005.01618.x |pmid=16411957 |bibcode=2006NewPh.169..549C |issn=0028-646X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Dropping leaves during the dry season is done to prevent water loss through [[transpiration]] out of the [[stoma]]ta, which would cause the water potentials in the vascular tissue to drop too low and pull water out of the [[vacuole]]s in the parenchyma cells. This would lead to the parenchyma cells, which make up the majority of the trunk and branches, to [[Plasmolysis|plasmolyse]] destroying the tree.<ref name=":1" />

Baobab trees have much higher water and parenchyma content than most trees, which allows them to grow very large with less energy expenditure.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Van den Bilcke |first1=N. |last2=De Smedt |first2=S. |last3=Simbo |first3=D. J. |last4=Samson |first4=R. |date=2013-09-01 |title=Sap flow and water use in African baobab (Adansonia digitata L.) seedlings in response to drought stress |journal=South African Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=88 |pages=438–446 |doi=10.1016/j.sajb.2013.09.006 |issn=0254-6299|doi-access=free |bibcode=2013SAJB...88..438V }}</ref> Parenchyma are soft plant tissue cells that are commonly used for water storage in other drought tolerant species like cactus and succulents. The water fluxes from the vascular tissue into the parenchyma cells at the center of the tree with the help of actively transported ions. The [[Flux|ion flux]] into the cell will shift the [[Molecular diffusion|concentration gradients]], causing water to rush into the cells for long-term storage.{{citation needed|date=June 2023}}

Another reason why the water in the trunk can only be used as a buffer for long-term deficits is the distance between the vascular tissue and the parenchyma. The transportation of water from the vascular tissue into storage cells is a very slow process as it is a high-resistance path.<ref name=":2" /> The water in the cells at the core of the trunk and the branches would take too much energy from the tree to move back into the vascular tissue for daily use.{{citation needed|date=June 2023}}

=== Bark ===
Baobab trees have a thick fibrous bark that possesses an exceptional capacity to heal from even severe damage. Unlike most trees, the depth of the bark (up to 8 cm in mature specimens) is due to thickening of the secondary phloem rather than the periderm, with the former accounting for 75% of the bark by volume. In addition to water storage, the abundance of parenchyma enhances the structural integrity of the tree, as they complement the phloem fibers to provide compressive and tensile strength, respectively. Moreover, a high density of parenchyma also contributes to the healing capacity of the bark, as these cells may undergo further division, and have some capacity to redifferentiate.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kotina |first=Ekaterina L. |last2=Oskolski |first2=Alexei A. |last3=Tilney |first3=Patricia M. |last4=Wyk |first4=Ben-Erik Van |date=June 2017 |title=Bark anatomy of Adansonia digitata L. (Malvaceae) |url=http://www.bioone.org/doi/10.5252/a2017n1a3 |journal=Adansonia |language=en |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=31–40 |doi=10.5252/a2017n1a3 |issn=1280-8571}}</ref>  The spongy material of the bark allows water to be absorbed deeper into the tissue, as there is rarely enough rain during the wet season to penetrate the litter layer of soil.<ref name=":1" />

The growth rate of baobab trees is determined by ground water or rainfall.<ref name="hank" /><ref name="red">{{cite journal |last1=Grové |first1=Naas |date=November 2011 |title=Redaksionele Kommentaar |url=http://www.dendro.co.za/uploads/2/8/2/1/2821110/dendron-digital.pdf |journal=Dendron |issue=43 |page=14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304035821/http://www.dendro.co.za/uploads/2/8/2/1/2821110/dendron-digital.pdf |archive-date=4 March 2016 |access-date=25 November 2015|language=af}}</ref> The trees produce faint growth rings, but counting growth rings is not a reliable way to age baobabs because some years a tree will form multiple rings and some years none.<ref name="Kornei">{{cite journal |last=Kornei |first=Katherine |date=12 Nov 2021 |title=Scientists determine the age of one of Africa's most famous trees |journal=Science|doi=10.1126/science.acx9629 |s2cid=244097751 |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/scientists-determine-age-one-africa-s-most-famous-trees|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The Panke baobab in [[Zimbabwe]] was around 2,450 years old when it died in 2011, making it the oldest [[angiosperm]] ever documented, and two other trees—Dorslandboom in [[Namibia]] and Glencoe in ==Taxonomy==
The scientific name ''Adansonia'' refers to the French explorer and botanist, [[Michel Adanson]] (1727–1806), who wrote the first botanical description for the full species.<ref name="Baum"/> The species name ''digitata'' refers to the digits of the hand, as the baobab has compound leaves with normally five (but up to seven) leaflets, akin to a hand.<ref name=dup>{{cite journal |last1=du Plessis |first1=Doep |title=Die Thabazimbi-bosveld se groot kremetart |journal=Dendron |date=November 2011 |issue=43 |page=11 |url=http://www.dendro.co.za/uploads/2/8/2/1/2821110/dendron-digital.pdf |access-date=25 November 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160304035821/http://www.dendro.co.za/uploads/2/8/2/1/2821110/dendron-digital.pdf |archive-date=4 March 2016 |language=af}}</ref> ''A. digitata'' is the [[type species]] of the genus ''Adansonia'' and is the only species in the section ''Adansonia''.<ref name="Baum"/> All species of ''Adansonia'' except ''A. digitata'' are [[diploid]]; ''A. digitata'' is [[tetraploid]].<ref name="kilima">{{cite journal |url=http://www.uq.edu.au/nuq/jack/Taxon%20new%20GPS.pdf |last=Pettigrew |first=J. D. |year=2012 |title=Morphology, ploidy and molecular phylogenetics reveal a new diploid species from Africa in the baobab genus ''Adansonia'' (Malvaceae: Bombacoideae) |journal=Taxon |volume=61 |issue=6 |pages=1240–1250 |display-authors=etal |doi=10.1002/tax.616006 |bibcode=2012Taxon..61.1240P |access-date=2022-03-12 |archive-date=2013-12-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131211185541/http://www.uq.edu.au/nuq/jack/Taxon%20new%20GPS.pdf }}</ref> Some populations of African baobab have significant genetic differences and it has been suggested that the taxon contains more than one species. For example, the shape of the fruit varies considerably from region to region.<ref name=braam>{{cite journal |last1=van Wyk |first1=Braam |title=Kommentaar oor die groot kremetart van Gannahoek |journal=Dendron |date=November 2011 |issue=43 |page=14 |url=http://www.dendro.co.za/uploads/2/8/2/1/2821110/dendron-digital.pdf |access-date=25 November 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304035821/http://www.dendro.co.za/uploads/2/8/2/1/2821110/dendron-digital.pdf |archive-date=4 March 2016 |language=af}}</ref> In Angola, the fruit are elongated, rather than round.<ref name="Baum"/>
A proposed new species (''Adansonia kilima'' Pettigrew, et al.), was described in 2012, found in high-elevation sites in eastern and southern Africa.<ref name="kilima"/> This is now however no longer considered a distinct species, but a synonym of ''A. digitata''.<ref name="cron"/> Some high-elevation trees in Tanzania show different genetics and morphology but further study is needed to determine if they should be considered a separate species.<ref name="cron"/>

=== History ===
The earliest written reports of African baobab are from a 14th-century travelogue by the Arab traveler [[Ibn Batuta]].<ref name="Baum" /> The first botanical description was by [[Prospero Alpini|Alpino]] (1592) looking at fruit that he observed in Egypt from an unknown source. They were called Bahobab, possibly from the Arabic "bu hibab", meaning "many-seeded fruit".<ref name="Baum" /> The French explorer and botanist, [[Michel Adanson]] observed a baobab tree in 1749 on the [[List of islands of Senegal|island of Sor, Senegal]], and wrote the first detailed botanical description of the full tree, accompanied with illustrations. Recognising the connection to the fruit described by Alpino he called the [[genus]] Baobab. [[Linnaeus]] later formally named the genus ''Adansonia'', to honour Adason, but use of baobab as the commonest vernacular name has persisted.<ref name="Baum" /> Additional common names include monkey-bread tree (the soft, dry fruit is edible), upside-down tree (the sparse branches resemble roots), and cream of tartar tree (cream of tartar) because of the powdery fruit pulp.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Monkey-bread tree (Adansonia digitata) {{!}} spotwild |url=https://spotwild.org/en/type/vmYmHq/monkey-bread-tree |access-date=2020-05-29 |website=spotwild.org |language=en |archive-date=2023-09-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230903044346/https://spotwild.org/en/type/vmYmHq/monkey-bread-tree }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The African baobab is associated with tropical savannas.<ref name="kempe"/> It is found in drier climates, is sensitive to water logging and frost and is not found in areas where sand is deep.<ref name="eol.org">{{cite encyclopedia|url=http://eol.org/pages/584789/details|title=Descriptions and articles about the Baobab (Adansonia digitata) - Encyclopedia of Life|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Life|access-date=17 May 2015}}</ref> It is native to mainland [[Africa]], between the latitudes 16° N and 26° S.<ref name= Patrut/> Some references consider it as introduced to [[Yemen]] and [[Oman]]<ref name="catalogueoflife.org"/> while others consider it native there.<ref name="kew"/> The tree has also been introduced to many other regions including [[Australia]] and [[Asia]].<ref name="auto2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2018-08-07/boabs-come-africa-baobabs-evolution/10060946|title=Curious Kimberley: Scientists disagree how boab trees got to Australia from Africa and Madagascar - ABC News|date=August 6, 2018|website=www.abc.net.au}}</ref>

The northern limit of its distribution in Africa is associated with rainfall patterns; only on the [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]] coast and in the [[Sudanian savanna]] does its occurrence venture naturally into the [[Sahel]]. On the Atlantic coast, this may be due to spreading after cultivation. Its occurrence is very limited in [[Central Africa]], and it is found only in the very north of [[South Africa]]. In [[East Africa]], the trees grow also in [[Scrubland|shrublands]] and on the coast. In [[Angola]] and [[Namibia]], the baobabs grow in woodlands, and in coastal regions, in addition to savannas.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://sec.org.in/jeevsampada/plantsindia/admin_dist.php?id=5694 |title=Adansonia digitata:Plant Database of India |access-date=21 March 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110826225647/http://sec.org.in/jeevsampada/plantsindia/admin_dist.php?id=5694|archive-date=26 August 2011}}</ref> The African Baobab is native to [[Mauritania]], [[Senegal]], [[Guinea]], [[Sierra Leone]], [[Mali]], [[Burkina Faso]], [[Ghana]], [[Togo]], [[Benin]], [[Niger]], [[Nigeria]], northern [[Cameroon]], [[Chad]], [[Sudan]], [[Republic of the Congo|Congo Republic]], [[Democratic Republic of the Congo|DR Congo]] (formerly Zaire), [[Eritrea]], [[Ethiopia]], southern [[Somalia]], [[Kenya]], [[Tanzania]], [[Zambia]], Zimbabwe, [[Malawi]], [[Mozambique]], [[Angola]], [[São Tomé Island|São Tomé]], [[Príncipe]], [[Annobón Province|Annobon]], [[South Africa]] (in Limpopo province, north of the Soutpansberg mountain range), Namibia, [[Botswana]].<ref name="catalogueoflife.org">{{cite web |url=http://www.catalogueoflife.org/col/details/species/id/27834ecae202acc3945ba338af5e1c20 |title=Catalogue of Life - ''Adansonia digitata'' L. |work=catalogueoflife.org |access-date=29 August 2017 |archive-date=20 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200220070938/http://www.catalogueoflife.org/col/details/species/id/27834ecae202acc3945ba338af5e1c20 }}</ref><ref name="eol.org"/> It is an introduced species in [[Java]], [[Nepal]], [[Sri Lanka]], [[Philippines]], [[Jamaica]], [[Puerto Rico]], [[Haiti]], [[Dominican Republic]], [[Venezuela]], [[Seychelles]], [[Comoros]], [[India]], [[Guangdong]], [[Fujian]], [[Yunnan]]<ref name="catalogueoflife.org"/> and has been planted in [[Penang]], Malaysia, along certain streets.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Gardner | first1=Simon | last2=Sitthisunthō̜n | first2=Phindā | last3=Lai | first3=Ee May | title=Heritage Trees of Penang | publisher=Areca books | publication-place=Penang | date=2011 | isbn=978-967-5719-06-6 | page=}}</ref> Arab traders introduced it to northwestern [[Madagascar]] where baobab trees were often planted at the center of villages.<ref name=wick/>

==Ecology==
All baobabs are [[deciduous]], losing their leaves in the dry season, and remaining leafless for about eight months of the year.<ref name="Baum"/> The African baobab is largely found in savannah habitats, which tend to be fire-prone. Adaptations to survive frequent fires include a thick and fire-resistant bark and thick-shelled fruit. Trees older than about 15 years have thick enough bark to withstand the heat of most savannah fires, while younger trees can resprout after fire.<ref name="kempe"/> The thick outer shell of the fruit may serve to protect the seeds.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wickens |first=G. E. |date=1982 |title=The Baobab: Africa's Upside-Down Tree |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4109961 |journal=Kew Bulletin |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=173–209 |doi=10.2307/4109961 |issn=0075-5974|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Pollination in the African baobab is achieved primarily by fruit bats, in West Africa mainly the [[straw-coloured fruit bat]], [[Gambian epauletted fruit bat]], and the [[Egyptian fruit bat]]. The flowers are also visited by [[galago]]s, and several kinds of insect.<ref name="Baum2">{{Cite journal|last=Baum|first=David A.|date=1995|title=The Comparative Pollination and Floral Biology of Baobabs (Adansonia- Bombacaceae)|journal=Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden|volume=82|issue=2|pages=322–348|doi=10.2307/2399883|jstor=2399883|bibcode=1995AnMBG..82..322B |issn=0026-6493}}</ref>

With their hard coat, baobab seeds can withstand drying and remain viable over long periods. The fruit is eaten by many species and the germination potential is improved when seeds have passed through the digestive tract of an animal, or have been subjected to fire.<ref name="Baum"/> [[Elephant]]s and [[baboon]]s are main dispersal agents<ref name="Baum"/> and so the seeds can potentially be dispersed over long distances. The fruit floats and the seeds are waterproof, so African baobabs may also be spread by water.<ref name="Baum"/> Some aspects of the baobab's reproductive biology are not yet understood but it is thought that pollen from another tree may be required to develop fertile seed. Isolated trees without a pollen source from another tree do form fruit, only to abort them at a later stage. The existence of some very isolated trees may then be due to their ability to disperse long distances but self-incompatibility.<ref name=braam/>

The fruit, bark, roots and leaves are a key food source for many animals and the trees themselves are an important source of shade and shelter.<ref name="Pennisi">{{cite web |last1=Pennisi |first1=Elizabeth |author-link=Elizabeth Pennisi |title=Africa's strangest trees are stranger than thought—and they're dying mysteriously. |url=https://www.science.org/ |access-date=12 March 2022 |website=Science News |publisher=Science}}</ref> [[Chimpanzee|Chimpanzees]] pound the seeds against the tree's branches and roots and rocks to open them in a "proto-tool use behavior".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Galán-Plana |first=Carlota F. |last2=Sánchez-Megías |first2=Andreu |last3=Renelies-Hamilton |first3=Justinn |last4=Llana |first4=Manuel |last5=Diallo |first5=Samba |last6=Barciela |first6=Amanda |last7=Dotras |first7=Laia |last8=Galbany |first8=Jordi |last9=Hernandez-Aguilar |first9=R. Adriana |date=2026 |title=New evidence of baobab (Adansonia digitata) pounding by western chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes verus) |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10329-026-01264-1 |journal=Primates |language=en |volume=67 |issue=4 |pages=375–386 |doi=10.1007/s10329-026-01264-1 |issn=0032-8332 |pmc=13283153 |pmid=42201530}}</ref>

== Conservation ==
The baobab is a protected tree in [[South Africa]],<ref name="dwaf">{{cite web |date=3 May 2013 |title=Protected Trees |url=http://www2.dwaf.gov.za/dwaf/cmsdocs/4116___poster%20protected%20trees.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100705085122/http://www2.dwaf.gov.za/dwaf/cmsdocs/4116___poster%20protected%20trees.pdf |archive-date=5 July 2010 |publisher=Department of Water Affairs and Forestry, Republic of South Africa}}</ref> and yet is threatened by various mining and development activities.<ref name="bega1">{{cite news |last1=Bega |first1=Sheree |date=20 March 2021 |title=Plan to uproot 100 000 trees in Limpopo 'sacrilege', says baobab expert |work=Environment |publisher=mg.co.za |agency=Mail & Guardian |url=https://mg.co.za/environment/2021-03-20-plan-to-uproot-100-000-trees-in-limpopo-sacrilege-says-baobab-expert/ |access-date=25 March 2021}}</ref> In the [[Sahel]], the effects of drought, [[desertification]] and over-use of the fruit have been cited as causes for concern.<ref name="osman">{{cite web |last1=Osman |first1=Siham M. |date=2014 |title=Save the Baobab |url=http://practicalaction.org/baobab |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151202045358/http://practicalaction.org/baobab |archive-date=2015-12-02 |access-date=6 December 2015 |website=practicalaction.org |publisher=ITDG Practical Action Sudan}}</ref> {{As of|2025|02}}, the African baobab is not yet classified by the [[IUCN Red List]], although there is evidence that populations may be declining. Many of the largest and oldest African baobabs have died in recent years.<ref name="Pennisi" /> [[Greenhouse gas]]es, [[climate change]], and [[global warming]] appear to be factors reducing baobab longevity.<ref name="yong">{{cite web |author1=Ed Yong |date=11 June 2018 |title=Trees That Have Lived for Millennia Are Suddenly Dying The oldest baobabs are collapsing, and there's only one likely explanation. |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/science/archive/2018/06/baobab-trees-dying-climate-change/562499/?single_page=true |access-date=12 June 2018 |publisher=The Atlantic}}</ref>

== Uses ==
[[File:Baobabcowherd.jpg|thumb|A cow-herder in [[Senegal]] harvests baobab leaves for forage in the dry season.]]
[[File:Baobab Frucht.jpg|thumb|upright|The fruit is used to make a drink.]]

People have traditionally valued the trees as sources of food, water, health remedies or places of shelter. The baobab is a [[traditional food]] plant in Africa, but is little-known elsewhere.<ref name=hank/> Adanson concluded that the baobab, of all the trees he studied, "is probably the most useful tree in all". He consumed baobab juice twice a day while in Africa, and was convinced that it maintained his health.<ref name="powbab.com">{{cite web |url= http://www.powbab.com/pages/the-baobab-tree|title=The Baobab Tree |work=Powbab |access-date=21 November 2015}}</ref> According to a modern field guide, the juice can help cure diarrhoea.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]], [[United States Department of the Army]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |page=26 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364}}</ref>

The roots and fruit are edible.<ref name=":0" /> The fruit has been suggested to have the potential to improve nutrition, boost food security, foster rural development and support sustainable land care.<ref>{{cite book |author=National Research Council |title=Lost Crops of Africa: Volume II: Vegetables |url=http://books.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=11763 |access-date=July 15, 2008 |volume=2 |date=October 27, 2006 |publisher=[[National Academies Press]] |isbn=978-0-309-10333-6 |doi= 10.17226/11763|chapter=Baobab |chapter-url=http://books.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=11763&page=75 }}</ref> In Sudan, where the tree is called ''tebeldi'' ({{Lang|ar|تبلدي}}), people make tabaldi juice by soaking and dissolving the dry pulp of the fruit in water, locally known as ''gunguleiz''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=A note on baobab (''Adansonia digitata'' L.) in Kordofan, Sudan | doi=10.1007/s10722-013-9964-5 |volume=60 |issue=4 |journal=Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution |pages=1587–1596 | last1 = Gebauer | first1 = J.| s2cid=6884609 |year = 2013| bibcode=2013GRCEv..60.1587G }}</ref> Water can also be extracted from some of the trunks.<ref name=":0" />

Baobab leaves can be eaten as a [[relish]]. Young fresh leaves are cooked in a sauce and sometimes are dried and powdered. The powder is called ''lalo'' in [[Mali]] and sold in many village markets in [[Western Africa]]. The leaves are used in the preparation of a soup termed ''miyan kuka'' in Northern Nigeria and are rich in phytochemicals and minerals.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ogbaga |first1=Chukwuma |last2=Nuruddeen |first2=Fatima |last3=Alonge |first3=Olatunbosun |last4=Nwagbara |first4=Onyinye |chapter= Phytochemical, elemental and proximate analyses of stored, sun-dried and shade-dried baobab (Adansonia digitata) leaves|title= 2017 13th International Conference on Electronics, Computer and Computation (ICECCO)|date=November 2017 |pages=1–5 |doi=10.1109/ICECCO.2017.8333339 |isbn=978-1-5386-2499-9 }}</ref> The seeds can be pounded into a flour<ref name=":0" /> or to extract oil for [[Cooking oil|cooking]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Sidibe |first1=M. |url=http://www.cropsforthefuture.org/publication/Monographs/Baobab%20Monograph.pdf |title=Baobab - Adansonia digitata |last2=Williams |first2=J. T. |publisher=International Centre for Underutilised Crops |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-85432-776-8 |location=Southampton, UK |pages=43, 48 |access-date=2012-07-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140506025824/http://www.cropsforthefuture.org/publication/Monographs/Baobab%20Monograph.pdf |archive-date=2014-05-06 }}</ref>
Baobab leaves are sometimes used as forage for ruminants in dry season. The oilmeal, which is a byproduct of oil extraction, can also be used as animal feed.<ref name="feedipedia">{{cite web | last1=Heuzé |first1=V. |last2=Tran |first2=G. |last3=Bastianelli |first3=D. |last4=Archimède |first4=H. | title = African baobab (''Adansonia digitata'') | url = https://www.feedipedia.org/node/525 | publisher = Feedipedia.org. A programme by [[INRA (France)|INRA]], [[CIRAD]], AFZ and [[FAO]] | date = January 25, 2013 | access-date = February 6, 2013}}</ref> Whole fruit, or just the fruit pulp, can be stored for months under dry conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=a Review on a Multipurpose Tree with Promising Future in the Sudan |url=https://www.pubhort.org/ejhs/2002/file_3713.pdf}}</ref>

The fibre from the bark can be used to make cloth.<ref name=shee>{{cite book|last1=Sheehan |first1=Sean |title=Zimbabwe (Vol. 6 of Cultures of the World) |date=2004 |publisher=Benchmark Books/Marshall Cavendish |location=New York |isbn=978-0-7614-1706-4 |page=13 |edition=2nd}}</ref> In times of drought, elephants consume the juicy wood beneath the bark of the baobab.<ref name="shee" />

===For export===
In 2008, the [[European Union]] approved the use and consumption of baobab fruit. It is commonly used as an ingredient in [[smoothie]]s and cereal bars.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.acnfp.gov.uk/assess/fullapplics/baobab |publisher=Advisory Committee on Novel Foods and Processes |title=Baobab dried fruit pulp |year=2008 |archive-url=http://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/20080603122942/http://www.acnfp.gov.uk/assess/fullapplics/baobab |archive-date=2008-06-03}}</ref> In 2009, the United States [[Food and Drug Administration]] granted [[generally recognised as safe]] status to baobab dried fruit pulp as a food ingredient.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.fda.gov/Food/FoodIngredientsPackaging/GenerallyRecognizedasSafeGRAS/GRASListings/ucm174945.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090904104304/http://www.fda.gov/Food/FoodIngredientsPackaging/GenerallyRecognizedasSafeGRAS/GRASListings/ucm174945.htm |archive-date=September 4, 2009 |publisher=[[Food and Drug Administration (United States)|FDA]] |title=Agency Response Letter GRAS Notice No. GRN 000273 |date=July 25, 2009 |author=Laura M. Tarantino}}</ref>

==In culture==
Along the [[Zambezi]], the tribes believed that baobabs were upright and too proud. The gods became angry and uprooted them and threw them back into the ground upside-down. Evil spirits now cause bad luck to anyone that picks up the sweet white flowers. More specifically, a lion will kill them.<ref name="krugerpark.co.za">{{cite web|url=http://www.krugerpark.co.za/africa_baobab.html |title=Boabab Tree - Southern African Trees - Adansonia digitata |work=krugerpark.co.za |access-date=17 May 2015}}</ref> In [[Kafue National Park]], one of the largest baobabs is known as "Kondanamwali" or the "tree that eats maidens". The tree fell in love with four beautiful maidens. When they reached puberty, they made the tree jealous by finding husbands. So, one night, during a thunderstorm, the tree opened its trunk and took the maidens inside. A rest house has been built in the branches of the tree. On stormy nights, the crying of the imprisoned maidens can still be heard.<ref name="krugerpark.co.za"/>

Some people believe that women living in [[kraal]]s where baobabs are plentiful will have more children. This belief is scientifically plausible as those women will have better access to the tree's vitamin-rich leaves and fruit to complement a vitamin-deficient diet.<ref name="krugerpark.co.za"/>

The tree also plays a role in [[Antoine de Saint-Exupéry|Antoine De Saint-Exupéry]]'s fictional children's book, ''[[The Little Prince]]''. In the story, baobabs are described as dangerous plants which must be weeded out from the good plants, lest they overcome a small planet and even break it to pieces.<ref>{{cite book |last=Saint-Exupéry |first=Antoine |title=Le Petit Prince |trans-title=[[The Little Prince]] |publisher=Reynal and Hitchcock |date=1943}}</ref>

=== Prominent specimens ===
{{GeoGroup}}
A number of individual baobab trees attract sightseers due to their age, size, history, location or isolated occurrence.{{citation needed|date=June 2023}}

==== Cape Verde ====
There is a large baobab tree in the town of Santa Maria on the island of Sal, Cape Verde islands.{{citation needed|date=June 2023}}

==== Botswana ====
Around [[Gweta]], Botswana, some have been declared national monuments. Green's Baobab, 27 km south of Gweta was inscribed by the 19th-century hunters and traders [[Frederick Thomas Green]] and Hendrik Matthys van Zyl besides other ruthless characters. Fred and Charles Green passed the baobab during an expedition to [[Lake Ngami]] and left the inscription "Green's Expedition 1858–1859". An earlier inscription by an unknown traveller reads "1771".<ref name="dac">{{cite web |title=The Historic Baobabs in Botswana |url=https://www.discoverafrica.com/blog/in-search-of-the-baobab-tree/ |website=discoverafrica.com |access-date=12 February 2020}}</ref>
About 11 km south of Green's Baobab is the turn-off to Chapman's Baobab, also known as Seven Sisters or Xaugam, i.e. "lion's tail" in [[Tshwa language|Tsoa]]. It was once an enormous multi-stemmed tree, used by passing explorers, traders and travellers as a navigation beacon. It guided them as they navigated the extensive salt pan northwards, while a hollow in the trunk served as a letterbox. The explorer and hunter [[James Chapman (explorer)|James Chapman]] left an engraving on a large root when he passed the tree with artist Thomas Baines in 1861, but [[David Livingstone|Livingstone]], [[William Cotton Oswell|Oswell]], [[Robert Moffat (missionary)|Moffat]], and [[Frederick Selous|Selous]] also camped here. Livingstone supposedly carved a cross and his initials, and conveyed his 1853 sojourn in ''Missionary Travels'', noting: "about two miles beyond [the immense saltpan Ntwetwe] we unyoked under a fine specimen of baobab, ... It consisted of 6 branches united into one trunk."<ref name="jd1">{{cite book |last1=Davidson |first1=Julie |title=Looking for Mrs Livingstone |date=2012 |publisher=Saint Andrew Press |isbn=978-0-7152-0964-6 |page=213}}</ref> It had a circumference of 25 m before its constituent trunks collapsed outward on 7 January 2016. Not all its trunks are confirmed dead however,{{citation needed|date=December 2022}} one showing signs of life in 2019.<ref name="glb1">{{cite web |last1=le Breton |first1=Gus |title=Is Chapman's Baobab Still Alive? Update from Botswana |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5PQBWcPggjw  |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211214/5PQBWcPggjw |archive-date=2021-12-14 |url-status=live|website=African Plant Hunter |date=29 October 2019 |publisher=YouTube |access-date=11 February 2020}}{{cbignore}}</ref>
Seven trees known as the Sleeping Sisters or Baines' Baobabs grow on a tiny islet in Kudiakam Pan, Botswana. They are named for [[Thomas Baines]] who painted them in May 1862,<!--original in Royal Geographical Society archives--> while en route to [[Victoria Falls]]. The fallen giant of Baines' day is still sprouting leaves (as of 2004), and a younger generation of trees are in evidence. The islet is accessible in winter when the pan is dry.<ref name="wats">{{cite book |last1=Watson |first1=Rupert |title=The African baobab |date=2007 |publisher=Struik |location=Cape Town |isbn=978-1-77007-430-9 |pages=190–191}}</ref>
Some large specimens have been transplanted to new sites, as was the one at Cresta Mowana lodge in [[Kasane]].<ref name=ash>{{cite web |last1=Ashby |first1=Alison |title=The baobab's secret |date=26 June 2013 |url=http://www.zambezitraveller.com/chobe/history/baobab%E2%80%99s-secret |website=zambezitraveller.com |access-date=25 November 2015 }}{{Dead link|date=October 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

==== Ghana ====
At Saakpuli (also Sakpele) in northern [[Ghana]] the site of a 19th-century [[slavery|slave]] transit camp is marked by a stand of large baobabs, to which slaves were chained.<ref name="bri">{{cite book|last1=Briggs|first1=Philip|title=Ghana: the Bradt travel guide |date=2014 |publisher=Bradt Travel Guides |location=Chalfont St. Peter, Bucks |isbn=978-1-84162-478-5 |page=427 |edition=6}}</ref> 

The chains were wrapped around their trunks or around the roots. Similarly, two trees at [[Salaga]] in central Ghana are reminders of the slave trade. One, located at the former slave market at the center of town, was replanted at the site of the original to which slaves were shackled. A second larger tree marks the slave cemetery, where bodies of dead slaves were dumped.{{citation needed|date=June 2023}}

==== India ====
Inside the [[Golconda Fort]] in [[Hyderabad]], India, is a baobab tree estimated to be 430 years old. It is the largest baobab outside of Africa.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/hyderabad/asi-conducts-health-check-up-of-430-year-old-baobab-tree-of-golconda-says-its-healthy/articleshow/65137289.cms|title=ASI conducts health check up of 430-year-old baobab tree of Golconda, says it's healthy |author=Syed Akbar|website=The Times of India|date=25 July 2018 |access-date=2019-04-15}}</ref>

==== Madagascar ====
[[File:The baobab, Mahajanga.jpg|thumb|right|250px|The baobab in [[Mahajanga]], Madagascar]]
The African baobab in [[Mahajanga]], Madagascar, had a circumference of {{Convert|21|m}} by 2013. It became the symbol of the city and was formerly a place for executions and important meetings.<ref name="sipa">{{cite web |last1=Sipa |first1=Masika |title=The Old Baobab of Mahajanga | date = 2013 |url=http://www.madamagazine.com/en/der-alte-baobab-von-mahajanga/ |website=madamagazine.com |publisher=MadaMagazine |access-date=24 July 2017}}</ref>

==== Mozambique ====
The Lebombo Eco Trail tree is about {{Convert abbreviated|18.5|m}} tall with a diameter of almost {{Convert abbreviated|22|m}}. It was found to be about 1400 years old and made up of five stems with ages between 900 and 1400 years, fused in a ring leaving a large central cavity.<ref name= Patrut/>

==== Namibia ====
The [[Ombalantu baobab tree|Ombalantu baobab]] in Namibia has a hollow trunk that can accommodate some 35 people. At times it has served as a chapel, post office, house, and hiding site. The Holboom baobab (Holboom, Nyae Nyae Conservancy, Namibia) is one of the trees with a hollow core. It measures {{Convert abbreviated|35.10|m}} around and radiocarbon dating shows it to be about 1750 years old.<ref name= Patrut/>

==== Senegal ====
The first botanical description of ''A. digitata'' was done by Adanson based on a tree on the island of Sor, Senegal. On the nearby [[Îles de la Madeleine (Senegal)|Îles des Madeleines]] Adanson found a baobab that was {{convert|3.8|m}} in diameter, which bore the carvings of passing mariners on its trunk, including those of [[Prince Henry the Navigator]] in 1444 and [[André Thevet]] in 1555.<ref name="wick" /> When [[Théodore Monod]] searched the island in the 20th century, this tree was not to be found. The Gouye Ndiouly or Guy Njulli <!--also Guy Ndiouli--> ("baobab of circumcision") may be the oldest baobab in Senegal and the northern hemisphere.<ref name="patrut2015">{{cite web |last1=Pătruţ |first1=prof. dr. Adrian (project manager) |title=New research in dendrochronology and environmental climate change by using AMS/CFAMS radiocarbon dating and stable isotope analysis |date = <!--January – December--> 2015 |url=http://chem.ubbcluj.ro/~apatrut/reports.php |website= chem.ubbcluj.ro |access-date=14 February 2020}}</ref> The partially collapsed tree from which new stems have emerged is situated near the bank of the [[Saloum River]] at [[Kahone]]. It was formerly the venue for the gàmmu, an annual festival during which the kingdom's provincial rulers pledged their loyalty to the king.<ref name="er1">{{cite web |last1=Ross |first1=Eric |title=Historic baobab trees of Senegal: Kahone |url= https://ericrossacademic.wordpress.com/2012/01/25/historic-baobab-trees-of-senegal/ |website=ericrossacademic.wordpress.com |date = 25 January 2012 |access-date=14 February 2020}}</ref> From 1593 to 1939, 49 kings of the Guélewars dynasty were inducted at this tree. It was beside the place where the Buur Saloum organised circumcision ceremonies,<ref name="patrut2015" /><ref name="sinesaloum">{{cite web |title=Kahone, Ancienne capitale du Saloum: Passé-présent d'une ville pluricentenaire |url= http://www.sinesaloum.info/kahone-ancienne-capitale-du-saloum-passe-present-d-une-ville-pluricentenaire.html |website= sinesaloum.info | date = 7 November 2016|access-date=14 February 2020}}</ref> and in 1862, it became the scene of a battle.

==== US Virgin Islands ====
[[File:BaobabTree20230926 100418.jpg|thumb|Grove Place Baobab on St. Croix.]]

The [[Grove Place, U.S. Virgin Islands|Grove Place]] Baobab, listed as a [[National Register of Champion Trees|Champion Tree]], is believed to be the oldest (250–300 years) of some 100 baobabs on [[Saint Croix]] in the [[United States Virgin Islands|US Virgin Islands]]. It is seen as a living testament to centuries of African presence, as the seeds were likely introduced by an African slave who arrived at the former estate during the 18th century. According to the bronze memorial plaque, twelve women were rounded up during the [[1878 St. Croix labor riot|1878 Fireburn labor riot]], and hanged beneath the tree. It has since been a rallying place for plantation laborers and unions.<ref name="nsc">{{cite web |title=New St. Croix Park Celebrates the Legacy of the Baobab Tree |url=https://repeatingislands.com/2009/05/30/new-st-croix-park-celebrates-the-legacy-of-the-baobab-tree/ |website=Repeating Islands |access-date=5 February 2020 |date=20 May 2009 |archive-date=5 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200205155607/https://repeatingislands.com/2009/05/30/new-st-croix-park-celebrates-the-legacy-of-the-baobab-tree/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==== Zimbabwe ====
Zimbabwe's Big Tree, near Victoria Falls, stands 25 metres tall and is visited by hundreds of thousands of tourists yearly. Radiocarbon dating has shown this one to be made up of several stems of various ages, with the oldest about 1150 years old.<ref name="Kornei"/>
